items.title: Inside View
items.question: A team estimates a project will take three months, reasoning only from the plan in front of them. Which forecasting error does this illustrate?
choices: The estimate came from the inside view
The estimate borrowed from finished projects
The estimate used a wide confidence range
The estimate ignored the current details
items.correctAnswer: The estimate came from the inside view
items.correctExplanation: Right. The team reasoned only from the plan's details rather than comparing with comparable finished work.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the estimate came from the inside view. The outside view would anchor on how long comparable work actually took.
items.lessonContent:
Plans are built from imagined steps.
Imagined steps rarely match lived ones.
Anchor estimates on completed comparable work.
Use your plan for detail, history for duration.
Share this: time one upcoming task against how long its twin took.

items.title: Reference Class
items.question: A supplier checks how long comparable orders took last year before quoting a delivery date. Which principle is being applied?
choices: Forecasting should start from similar past cases
Forecasting should ignore all previous orders
Forecasting should trust only the latest order
Forecasting should begin with the largest order
items.correctAnswer: Forecasting should start from similar past cases
items.correctExplanation: Right. Comparing against a group of comparable completed jobs grounds the estimate in evidence.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: forecasting should start from similar past cases. A group of precedents corrects the optimism of a single imagined plan.
items.lessonContent:
A reference class turns anecdotes into evidence.
Choose the class carefully; too broad misleads.
Compare like with like, then adjust.
Precedent beats prediction when history is rich.
Share this: build a small reference class for one decision today.

items.title: Hofstadters Rule
items.question: Everyone knows that projects overrun, yet each team still promises it will finish exactly on schedule. Which rule names this pattern?
choices: Knowing delays recur, we still expect to finish on time
Knowing delays recur, we pad every estimate
Knowing delays recur, we cancel every project
Knowing delays recur, we finish ahead of plan
items.correctAnswer: Knowing delays recur, we still expect to finish on time
items.correctExplanation: Right. The rule captures how awareness of overruns never seems to correct the next promise.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: knowing delays recur, we still expect to finish on time. Each team treats its own plan as the exception to a rule it fully accepts.
items.lessonContent:
Awareness of a bias does not remove it.
Self-exemption is the hidden move.
Apply the base rate to your own case too.
Assume the overrun, then plan around it.
Share this: add an explicit buffer to one estimate today.

items.title: Optimism Bias
items.question: A study finds that most renovation projects cost more and please less than their owners expected. Which bias does this describe?
choices: We underestimate costs and overestimate benefits
We overestimate costs and underestimate benefits
We estimate costs and benefits perfectly
We ignore both costs and benefits entirely
items.correctAnswer: We underestimate costs and overestimate benefits
items.correctExplanation: Right. The pattern is systematic: outlays surprise upward while payoffs disappoint downward.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: we underestimate costs and overestimate benefits. Planning would improve if the base rate, not the hope, set the starting point.
items.lessonContent:
Forecasts skew toward the outcome we want.
Systematic error distorts whole industries.
Use base rates as the neutral anchor.
Discount your own rosy estimate by default.
Share this: revise one budget tonight using the base rate instead.

items.title: Premortem Habit
items.question: Before launching, a team imagines the project has failed and writes down every plausible cause. What does this exercise achieve?
choices: Imagining failure in advance surfaces hidden risks
Imagining failure in advance guarantees success
Imagining failure in advance wastes the team's time
Imagining failure in advance replaces the plan
items.correctAnswer: Imagining failure in advance surfaces hidden risks
items.correctExplanation: Right. Assuming the failure has already happened frees people to name worries they would otherwise suppress.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: imagining failure in advance surfaces hidden risks. The technique does not predict doom but enlarges the list of things worth watching.
items.lessonContent:
Dissent is easier when the outcome is already assumed.
Naming risks lowers their surprise value.
A premortem converts silence into a checklist.
Practise the failure before living it.
Share this: run a five-minute premortem before your next big step.

items.title: Buffer Eaten
items.question: A manager adds slack to a schedule, and the extra time quietly disappears into small additions. What is the lesson?
choices: Padding a plan can be absorbed by scope creep
Padding a plan always shortens the project
Padding a plan removes every hidden risk
Padding a plan eliminates the need to plan
items.correctAnswer: Padding a plan can be absorbed by scope creep
items.correctExplanation: Right. Extra time is a resource that unplanned work tends to consume unless it is fenced off.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: padding a plan can be absorbed by scope creep. Slack only protects the deadline if new demands are refused or traded.
items.lessonContent:
Slack is a resource and can be spent.
Unfenced buffer invites extra work.
Protect reserve by trading, not adding.
Name what the buffer is for.
Share this: declare today what one reserve must not be used for.

items.title: Range Not Date
items.question: Asked when a task will finish, an experienced planner gives a best and worst case rather than one date. Why?
choices: A range is more honest than a single date
A range hides the planner's uncertainty
A range is always wider than reality
A range means the planner has no idea
items.correctAnswer: A range is more honest than a single date
items.correctExplanation: Right. A range expresses the real uncertainty that a single number falsely hides.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a range is more honest than a single date. Precision that outruns evidence is a promise the planner cannot keep.
items.lessonContent:
Uncertainty is information, not weakness.
Single numbers overstate knowledge.
Give bounds and state confidence.
Let ranges guide buffers and decisions.
Share this: express one estimate today as a range instead of a point.

items.title: Back to Average
items.question: A firm celebrated a record sales month, and the next month was ordinary. What statistical effect explains this?
choices: An extreme result tends to drift back toward average
An extreme result always repeats exactly
An extreme result means the firm is failing
An extreme result cannot be measured at all
items.correctAnswer: An extreme result tends to drift back toward average
items.correctExplanation: Right. Very high or low outcomes usually reflect some luck that does not persist.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: an extreme result tends to drift back toward average. Reading the return as failure, or the peak as a new normal, misreads random noise.
items.lessonContent:
Extremes contain luck as well as signal.
Expect regression after unusual results.
Judge interventions against the expected drift.
Do not treat noise as a trend.
Share this: note tonight an extreme result and predict its likely drift.

items.title: After the Fact
items.question: Once an election result is known, commentators say the outcome was obvious all along. Which bias is at work?
choices: We call outcomes predictable only after they happen
We predict outcomes accurately before they happen
We remember only the most unlikely outcomes
We ignore outcomes that already happened
items.correctAnswer: We call outcomes predictable only after they happen
items.correctExplanation: Right. Hindsight rewrites memory so that the known outcome feels as if it had been foreseeable.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: we call outcomes predictable only after they happen. The cure is to write down predictions before events unfold and score them later.
items.lessonContent:
Memory is edited by what we now know.
Hindsight conceals genuine uncertainty.
Record forecasts before the fact.
Score them to calibrate judgement.
Share this: write one prediction today with a date to check it.

items.title: Recent and Vivid
items.question: After a plane crash dominates the news, travellers overestimate the danger of flying. Which factor is distorting their judgement?
choices: Vivid recent events distort probability estimates
Air travel is actually becoming deadlier
News reports always understate real risks
Statistics are irrelevant to every decision
items.correctAnswer: Vivid recent events distort probability estimates
items.correctExplanation: Right. Easy recall makes a rare event feel common, so frequency is judged by memory rather than data.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: vivid recent events distort probability estimates. Base rates, not headlines, give the true frequency.
items.lessonContent:
Judged frequency follows ease of recall.
Dramatic coverage inflates perceived risk.
Return to base rates when emotions spike.
Notice what memory is doing to your maths.
Share this: check a real base rate against a recent scare tonight.

items.title: First Number Trap
items.question: A negotiator opens with an extreme figure, and the final deal lands near it. What effect is being exploited?
choices: The first number drags the whole forecast
The last number decides the whole deal
Numbers have no effect on negotiations
Extreme figures always end negotiations
items.correctAnswer: The first number drags the whole forecast
items.correctExplanation: Right. An initial figure becomes an anchor, and later adjustments stay tethered to it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the first number drags the whole forecast. The defence is to prepare your own number and test whether it is reasonable independently.
items.lessonContent:
Anchors pull estimates toward themselves.
Even implausible numbers leave a trace.
Set your own reference before listening.
Adjust from evidence, not from their opening.
Share this: decide your number before hearing anyone else's.

items.title: Past Spending
items.question: A company keeps funding a failing product because it has already invested heavily. Which trap is this?
choices: Past spending should not decide future steps
Past spending should always guide future steps
Future spending justifies the past completely
Spending decisions cannot ever be reconsidered
items.correctAnswer: Past spending should not decide future steps
items.correctExplanation: Right. Money already gone cannot be recovered, so only future costs and benefits should steer the decision.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: past spending should not decide future steps. Letting sunk costs rule is throwing good resources after bad.
items.lessonContent:
Sunk costs cannot be recovered.
Decide from what lies ahead, not behind.
Losses make quitting feel like waste.
Reframe: the waste already happened.
Share this: name one commitment you would refuse if starting fresh today.

items.title: Many Futures
items.question: A strategist draws several distinct possible futures and plans responses for each, rather than betting on one prediction. What is this approach?
choices: Preparing several futures beats one prediction
Preparing several futures confuses the whole team
Preparing several futures replaces all decisions
Preparing several futures guarantees the best one
items.correctAnswer: Preparing several futures beats one prediction
items.correctExplanation: Right. Robustness across scenarios matters more than being right about a single forecast.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: preparing several futures beats one prediction. Scenarios expose which choices survive regardless of which future arrives.
items.lessonContent:
Prediction is fragile; preparation is robust.
Consider a few divergent futures.
Look for choices that win in most of them.
Hedge what cannot be decided now.
Share this: sketch two futures that would change one plan of yours.

items.title: Biggest Unknown
items.question: A project carries one large unknown and many minor ones. Where should effort go first?
choices: Retire the biggest uncertainty first
Polish the smallest details first
Ignore uncertainty until launch day
Add staff to every uncertain area
items.correctAnswer: Retire the biggest uncertainty first
items.correctExplanation: Right. Resolving the largest unknown changes the plan most, so it deserves the earliest attention.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: retire the biggest uncertainty first. Polishing minor details while the core risk remains is comfort work, not progress.
items.lessonContent:
Uncertainty has weight as well as count.
Tackle the question that could sink the plan.
Information has value when it changes action.
Spend early effort on the decisive unknown.
Share this: name the single unknown that most changes your current plan.

items.title: Short Record
items.question: A new restaurant has been busy for two weeks, and an investor projects a decade of growth from that. What is the flaw?
choices: A short track record cannot anchor a forecast
A short track record guarantees future growth
A long track record is always misleading
Restaurants cannot be forecast at all
items.correctAnswer: A short track record cannot anchor a forecast
items.correctExplanation: Right. Two weeks is dominated by novelty and luck, not by a stable trend.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a short track record cannot anchor a forecast. Small samples vary wildly, so long-range claims need much more history.
items.lessonContent:
Small samples swing widely.
Early success often reflects novelty.
Extend the window before extrapolating.
Separate a spark from a steady flame.
Share this: ask how much data underlies one confident projection you hear.

items.title: Rare and Huge
items.question: Standard models gave no warning before a market collapse that almost nobody foresaw. Which idea captures this?
choices: Rare high-impact events are missed by normal models
Rare high-impact events are always predicted early
Normal models capture every extreme event
Markets collapse on a fixed schedule
items.correctAnswer: Rare high-impact events are missed by normal models
items.correctExplanation: Right. Tools tuned to ordinary variation understate the tails, where the largest shocks live.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: rare high-impact events are missed by normal models. Risk work must consider extremes outside the familiar range.
items.lessonContent:
Models fit the middle, not the tails.
Rare events carry outsized consequences.
Plan for plausibility, not just frequency.
Keep slack for the unmodelled.
Share this: identify one low-probability event worth a contingency.

items.title: Other People Delay
items.question: A manager is confident their own team will hit the deadline but assumes every other team will slip. What is this?
choices: We see others delays but not our own
We see our own delays but not others
No one ever delays in large projects
Delays are always caused by suppliers
items.correctAnswer: We see others delays but not our own
items.correctExplanation: Right. The same optimism that seems obvious in others stays invisible when turned inward.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: we see others delays but not our own. Applying the observed base rate to one's own team is the correction.
items.lessonContent:
We judge others by history and ourselves by hope.
The bias hides in the blind spot.
Apply the same rate to your own work.
Assume your team will face the common friction.
Share this: predict a delay for your own task before others do.

items.title: Quiet Additions
items.question: A project's deadline holds while a stream of small requested features accumulates. What is happening?
choices: Small additions quietly expand the original plan
Small additions reduce the total amount of work
Small additions are always cost-free choices
Small additions finish projects ahead of time
items.correctAnswer: Small additions quietly expand the original plan
items.correctExplanation: Right. Each request looks minor alone, but together they consume the schedule and the buffer.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: small additions quietly expand the original plan. Scope must be defended deliberately or it drifts.
items.lessonContent:
Scope grows by increments, not announcements.
Each small yes has a hidden cost.
Track additions explicitly.
Trade scope against time or quality.
Share this: total the small additions you accepted this week.

items.title: Too Many Hands
items.question: A leader doubles the team size expecting the project to finish twice as fast, but it slows down. Why?
choices: More people can slow a project rather than speed it
More people always double the project's speed
Team size never affects any project
Smaller teams cannot finish any project
items.correctAnswer: More people can slow a project rather than speed it
items.correctExplanation: Right. Coordination and communication grow faster than headcount, eating the expected gain.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: more people can slow a project rather than speed it. Beyond a point, onboarding and meetings outweigh added output.
items.lessonContent:
Coordination cost grows with each pair of people.
Adding hands adds communication channels.
Check whether work can be partitioned cleanly.
Sometimes shrinking the team speeds delivery.
Share this: count how much of a recent meeting was coordination.

items.title: Static Assumption
items.question: A pricing plan assumes customers will not change their behaviour after the change. What is the weakness?
choices: Plans that assume a static world ignore reactions
Plans that assume a static world are always right
Customers never respond to price changes
Pricing plans cannot be evaluated at all
items.correctAnswer: Plans that assume a static world ignore reactions
items.correctExplanation: Right. People respond to new rules, so the world after the change differs from the world used to design it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: plans that assume a static world ignore reactions. Good planning asks how others will respond once the plan is live.
items.lessonContent:
Interventions change the system they enter.
People adapt to new rules quickly.
Model reactions, not just the first move.
Ask how the plan looks a year in.
Share this: name one group whose response could change your plan.

items.title: Worst Case Floor
items.question: A disaster planner asks what the worst realistic outcome is and prepares supplies for it. What does this achieve?
choices: Considering the worst case sets a floor for response
Considering the worst case predicts the exact outcome
Considering the worst case prevents all bad events
Considering the worst case wastes limited resources
items.correctAnswer: Considering the worst case sets a floor for response
items.correctExplanation: Right. Preparing for the worst defines a minimum capability, even though the exact event remains unknown.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: considering the worst case sets a floor for response. It does not forecast one scenario but guarantees a baseline of readiness.
items.lessonContent:
Preparedness is measured against the extreme.
A floor is more useful than a forecast.
Define the minimum acceptable response.
Check feasibility before committing.
Share this: name the worst plausible outcome for one plan you hold.

items.title: False Precision
items.question: A forecast states revenue will reach exactly 4,317,000 next year. What is the main problem?
choices: Precision is asserted without evidence
Rounding numbers always destroys meaning
Revenue cannot be measured at all
Exact numbers are always more honest
items.correctAnswer: Precision is asserted without evidence
items.correctExplanation: Right. False exactness implies knowledge the forecaster cannot possibly possess.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: precision is asserted without evidence. Honest forecasts give ranges and state their confidence.
items.lessonContent:
Exact digits imply exact knowledge.
False precision misleads decision makers.
Round to the confidence you actually have.
Signal uncertainty openly.
Share this: round one wildly specific figure you meet today.

items.title: Road Not Taken
items.question: A company judges a decision only by how the chosen path turned out, ignoring the paths it never tried. Which error is this?
choices: Judging only the path taken hides the alternatives
The chosen path always reveals the truth
Alternatives are irrelevant to any decision
Outcomes never inform good judgement
items.correctAnswer: Judging only the path taken hides the alternatives
items.correctExplanation: Right. The unchosen options remain unknown, so the outcome alone cannot prove the decision was wise or foolish.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: judging only the path taken hides the alternatives. Good evaluation reconstructs what was likely under the roads not taken.
items.lessonContent:
Outcomes are noisy measures of decisions.
The counterfactual also had possibilities.
Judge the process, not just the result.
Imagine how the other path might have fared.
Share this: assess one past choice by its reasoning, not only its result.

items.title: Filling the Time
items.question: A task that could be done in a day is given a week, and it takes the whole week. Which principle is this?
choices: Work expands to fill the available time
Work shrinks to fit the available time
Deadlines have no effect on the work
Short deadlines always improve quality
items.correctAnswer: Work expands to fill the available time
items.correctExplanation: Right. Generous time invites over-elaboration and delays until the deadline forces completion.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: work expands to fill the available time. Tight but realistic limits can focus effort without harming quality.
items.lessonContent:
Time available shapes effort, not just capacity.
Deadlines ration attention.
Set durations deliberately, not generously.
Watch for polish that adds no value.
Share this: shorten one deadline modestly and observe the result.

items.title: Tracking Accuracy
items.question: A forecaster records predictions and later checks how often the confident ones were right. What is being improved?
choices: Track forecasts to learn how wrong you tend to be
Track forecasts to guarantee future accuracy
Track forecasts to avoid making more of them
Track forecasts to impress other people
items.correctAnswer: Track forecasts to learn how wrong you tend to be
items.correctExplanation: Right. Feedback turns vague confidence into a measurable calibration that can be corrected.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: track forecasts to learn how wrong you tend to be. Keeping score is how judgement learns its own biases.
items.lessonContent:
Unmeasured judgement cannot improve.
Feedback converts confidence into data.
Keep a record of predictions and outcomes.
Adjust your confidence from the score.
Share this: log one prediction tonight and set a date to check it.
